message.content:
The three most widely‑recognized “great” schisms in Christian history are:

| # | Schism | Approximate dates | Key parties involved | Main outcome |
|---|--------|-------------------|----------------------|--------------|
| 1 | **Great Schism of 1054** (East–West Schism) | 1054 CE | Eastern (Byzantine) Church vs. Western (Roman) Church | Formal split into the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches; the two traditions have remained separate ever since. |
| 2 | **Protestant Reformation** | 1517 – 1648 CE | Martin Luther, John Calvin, Henry VIII, and other reformers vs. the Roman Catholic Church | Birth of the major Protestant denominations (Lutheran, Reformed/Calvinist, Anglican, etc.) and a lasting division between Protestant and Catholic Christianity. |
| 3 | **East–West Schism of the 16th–17th centuries** (often called the *Reformation‑era schism* or *Schism of the 16th century*) | 16th – 17th centuries | Various national churches (e.g., the Church of England, the Dutch Reformed Church, the Swiss Reformed Church) vs. the Roman Catholic Church | Further fragmentation of Western Christianity into multiple national and theological traditions, solidifying the Protestant‑Catholic divide. |

> **Note:** The third entry is sometimes grouped with the Protestant Reformation, but it is often treated as a distinct schism because it involved the formal establishment of national churches that were not simply branches of the existing Catholic hierarchy. In many historical surveys, the “Great Schisms” are listed as the 1054 East–West split, the 16th‑century Protestant Reformation, and the subsequent national‑church schisms that followed the Reformation.
